title: Bits: Sum of Two Integers Without + or -
oneLiner: Add like a circuit does: XOR is the sum without carries, AND shifted left is the carry, and you repeat until there's no carry left.
keyTakeaway: a ^ b adds each bit position ignoring carries; (a & b) << 1 is exactly the carries, moved to the column they carry into. Replace a with the first and b with the second until b is 0. In C# this just works on 32-bit ints, negatives included. In Python, ints have no fixed width, so mask every step with 0xFFFFFFFF and convert the final 32-bit pattern back to a signed value.
explanation:
Return a + b for two 32-bit signed integers without using + or - (the tests can't check that, so it's on your honour). The result should behave like 32-bit int arithmetic: 2,147,483,647 + 1 wraps round to -2,147,483,648, as it does in C# by default.

Binary addition by hand: in each column, 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1. The digit you write down is 1 exactly when the two bits differ, which is XOR. A carry happens exactly when both bits are 1, which is AND, and the carry lands one column to the left, which is << 1. So a + b = (a ^ b) + ((a & b) << 1). That still has a +, but the carry part has moved left, so repeat: set a = a ^ b and b = (a & b) << 1 (computed from the old values) until b is 0. Each round pushes the carries at least one column further left, so at most 32 rounds, O(1). This is what a ripple-carry adder in a CPU does with logic gates (see Logic Gates in Computer Fundamentals).

Negative numbers. Two's complement stores -k as the bit pattern of 2^32 - k, and the point of that encoding is that ordinary binary addition gives the right answer for negatives too. In C#, int is exactly 32 bits, the carry out of bit 31 simply falls off, and the loop handles every case unchanged.

Python is the trap. Python ints have unlimited width, and a negative int behaves as if it had infinitely many 1 bits on the left. With a negative input the carry keeps marching left for ever and the loop never ends. Fix it by working in 32 bits explicitly: AND every intermediate result with 0xFFFFFFFF (32 one bits), which throws away everything above bit 31. At the end the answer is an unsigned pattern from 0 to 2^32 - 1; if it's above 0x7FFFFFFF (bit 31 set, so negative in two's complement), convert it with ~(a ^ 0xFFFFFFFF), which flips the low 32 bits twice and the infinite high bits once, sign-extending it. (a - 2**32 also works, but uses a minus.)

The visualization adds 5 + 3 in 4-bit rows.

visualizationSteps.message: a = 5 (0101), b = 3 (0011). Each round: a becomes a ^ b (sum without carries) and b becomes (a & b) << 1 (the carries, moved one column left).
a ^ b = 0110, (a & b) << 1 = 0010. Still 2 to add in.
a ^ b = 0100, (a & b) << 1 = 0100. Still 4 to add in.
a ^ b = 0000, (a & b) << 1 = 1000. Still 8 to add in.
a ^ b = 1000, (a & b) << 1 = 0000. No carries left.
b is 0, so a = 8 is the sum: 5 + 3 = 8, after 4 rounds.

recognitionSignals: "Without using + or -" or "without arithmetic operators": rebuild the operation from bitwise ones.
Questions about how hardware adds, or why two's complement makes negative addition free.
Any bit loop on possibly negative numbers in Python: think about masking to a fixed width.
gotchas: Compute the carry from the OLD a and b: in C# use a temporary (var carry = (a & b) << 1; a ^= b; b = carry;).
In Python, without masking with 0xFFFFFFFF a negative input loops for ever, and the final value must be sign-extended back from 32 bits.
In C#, if you use >> anywhere on negatives remember it's an arithmetic shift; this solution only needs <<.
confusableWith: Single Number (this track) uses XOR alone, as "addition with no carries" that makes pairs cancel; here the carries matter and AND plus a shift supplies them.
Multiplying without * is the same idea one level up: shift-and-add over the bits of one operand, like fast exponentiation uses shift-and-multiply.

complexity.note: Each round moves the carries at least one column left, so a 32-bit add takes at most 32 rounds: constant for fixed-width ints.
